topic: Connection grant type for an internal-only app
stem: Orchard Freight wants signers to have their shipment rate codes checked against the company's in-house rates service, which sits behind the corporate identity provider. The information security team allows only machine-to-machine access to that service: no person may ever sign in interactively to authorize a connection. The app will be used only by Orchard's own two production accounts and will never be offered to other companies. The service is written in Java and hosted in a private cloud. Which registration choices should the developer make?

options.text: Set the distribution to PUBLIC and choose the Client Credentials grant for the connection, limiting the publication regions to those where Orchard's accounts are hosted
Set the distribution to PRIVATE and choose the Authorization Code grant, asking the identity team for a service user that an admin signs in as once when connecting
Set the distribution to PRIVATE and choose the Client Credentials grant for the connection, then share the live app with Orchard's two production accounts
Set the distribution to PRIVATE and leave the connection unauthenticated, letting the rates service trust calls signed with Orchard's Docusign integration key

answerText: Set the distribution to PRIVATE and choose the Client Credentials grant for the connection, then share the live app with Orchard's two production accounts
explanation: The connection grant type can be Authorization Code or Client Credentials, and Client Credentials can be selected only when the distribution is Private. 'Only machine-to-machine access' plus 'only Orchard's own accounts' therefore means Private with Client Credentials.
whyNotOthers: C is right because Client Credentials gives the no-interactive-login connection the security team demands, and it is only available for privately distributed apps. The trap is A: Client Credentials is not available with PUBLIC distribution, and limiting regions does not change that. B breaks the rule that no person signs in interactively, and D is wrong because the connection is how Docusign obtains authorization to the external service; a Docusign integration key plays no part in it.

optionExplanations.A: Client Credentials can only be selected when the distribution type is Private, and a public listing is not what Orchard wants anyway.
optionExplanations.B: Authorization Code requires someone to sign in to authorize the connection, which the security team forbids.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. Private distribution unlocks the Client Credentials grant, which needs no interactive sign-in, and sharing limits use to Orchard's accounts.
optionExplanations.D: The connection holds the authorization details for the external service; a Docusign integration key does not authenticate Docusign's calls to it.

decode.needs: A private extension app whose connection uses the Client Credentials grant
clues: only machine-to-machine access, no person signs in -> Client Credentials grant
only our own two production accounts -> PRIVATE distribution
Java, private cloud -> red herring

concept.title: Client Credentials requires private distribution
concept.line: Extension app connections use Authorization Code or Client Credentials; Client Credentials is selectable only for privately distributed apps.

stem: Beacon Staffing is building an onboarding workflow in which the candidate's profile is pulled from the company's HR platform to prefill an intake form before the offer letter is signed. The HR platform is the system of record, and the information security review will reject any app registration that declares the ability to write back to it: data may flow out of HR, never in. The workflow runs in the company's own account, and the HR vendor exposes a REST API. How should the developer implement the extension app?

options.text: Implement all five Data IO actions and have Create Record and Patch Record return an error, so that any write attempted at runtime is rejected by the HR platform
Implement Get Type Names, Get Type Definitions and Create Record, because the type actions describe the HR data and Create Record returns it to the workflow
Register a connected fields extension so the intake form fields are autofilled from the HR platform at the moment the candidate opens the form
Register a Data IO extension with the Data Read option, implementing only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions

answerText: Register a Data IO extension with the Data Read option, implementing only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions
explanation: Data input can be implemented on its own: a read-only Data IO app implements only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions (Data Read in the form). Because the review rejects 'any registration that declares the ability to write', write actions must not be declared at all.
whyNotOthers: D is right because Data IO supports read-only registration with just the three read actions, so no write capability is declared. The trap is A: erroring at runtime still declares the write actions, which the stated security review rejects. B misuses Create Record, which writes a new record rather than reading one, and C is wrong because connected fields work in eSignature envelopes, not in prefilling workflow forms from a system of record.

optionExplanations.A: Declaring all five actions declares write capability, which is exactly what the security review rejects; runtime errors do not change the registration.
optionExplanations.B: Create Record creates entries in the system of record; reading data uses Search Records.
optionExplanations.C: Connected fields verify and autofill eSignature envelope fields; reading a system of record into a workflow is the Data IO extension.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Data input is a standalone capability: Search Records plus the two type actions (Data Read) read without declaring any write.

decode.needs: A Data IO extension registered for reading only
clues: prefill an intake form inside the workflow from HR -> Data IO data read step
review rejects any registration declaring write -> do not implement Create or Patch Record
HR vendor exposes REST -> red herring

concept.title: Data IO can be read-only
concept.line: A read-only Data IO app implements only Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions; writing requires all five actions.

topic: Data IO action when no record matches
stem: A Maestro data write step runs, but its query finds no matching record in the system of record. Which Data IO action does Docusign invoke to store the data?

options.text: Patch Record
Create Record
Search Records
Get Type Definitions

explanation: Create Record runs when a data output step is executed and no query is provided or the query does not find a record to update.
whyNotOthers: B is right because Create Record handles the 'nothing found' case of a write step. The trap is A: Patch Record runs only when the query finds an existing record. C is the lookup that came back empty, not the write, and D runs when a connection is established or refreshed.

optionExplanations.A: Patch Record updates an existing entry and runs only when the query finds a record.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. With no query or no match, the write step creates a new entry with Create Record.
optionExplanations.C: Search Records performs the lookup that found nothing; it does not store data.
optionExplanations.D: Get Type Definitions runs when a connection is created or refreshed to describe the data model.

concept.title: Create versus Patch in Data IO
concept.line: A data write step patches the record its query finds; with no query or no match, it creates a new record.

topic: Enforcing bank account verification during signing
stem: Lakeside Credit Union sends auto loan disbursement forms in which the borrower types a US checking account number and ABA routing number. Compliance requires that the borrower cannot finish signing unless those details pass a check with the credit union's bank-data provider. Who owns the account is not part of this check, because identity is confirmed in a separate know-your-customer step earlier in the process. Loan officers send the forms from the eSignature web app, and each envelope also carries a rate disclosure PDF. Which two choices meet the requirement? (Select two)

options.text: Select Must verify to sign on the verification fields so the borrower cannot complete the envelope until the bank-data check succeeds
Leave Must verify to sign unchecked, because verification still runs and prompts the borrower to correct invalid details before completing
Use the bank account owner verification extension so the provider confirms both the account details and that the borrower owns the account
Add a Data IO read step to a Maestro workflow that searches the bank-data provider for the account number before the envelope is sent out
Use bank account verification extension fields on the template so the account and routing number are checked as they are entered

answerText: Select Must verify to sign on the verification fields so the borrower cannot complete the envelope until the bank-data check succeeds; Use bank account verification extension fields on the template so the account and routing number are checked as they are entered
explanation: Bank account verification (Verify.Version3.BankAccount) checks the account and routing details in real time during signing, and Must verify to sign makes successful verification a condition of completing. 'Cannot finish signing unless' is the enforcement clue; 'who owns the account is not part of this check' rules out the owner extension.
whyNotOthers: A and E are right: the bank account verification extension performs the check, and Must verify to sign enforces it. The trap is B: if Must verify to sign is left unchecked, verification still occurs but successful verification is not required to complete signing, so it only records rather than enforces. C adds an ownership check the stem explicitly excludes, and D runs in a Maestro workflow before sending, not while the borrower signs, and Data IO is not a verification extension.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Must verify to sign requires successful verification of the supplied data before the signing process can be completed.
optionExplanations.B: Unchecked, verification still occurs, but completing the envelope no longer depends on it; the requirement is enforcement.
optionExplanations.C: Bank account owner verification also confirms ownership or authorized signatory, which the stem says is handled elsewhere and is not required.
optionExplanations.D: Data IO reads or writes a system of record in Maestro workflows; it does not check what the borrower types during signing.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. The bank account verification extension checks US ABA account details in real time as the recipient fills in the fields.

decode.needs: Bank account verification fields with Must verify to sign selected
clues: cannot finish signing unless the check passes -> Must verify to sign
who owns the account is not part of the check -> bank account verification, not owner verification
sent from the web app, extra disclosure PDF -> red herrings

concept.title: Must verify to sign enforces verification
concept.line: Data verification runs either way; selecting Must verify to sign makes successful verification a condition for completing signing.

topic: Fixing an app that is in review
stem: Amara submitted the first version of her company's extension app for Docusign review yesterday, and the Developer Console shows it as In Review. This morning QA found that one action still points at the old endpoint path in its params.uri. Amara wants the version that Docusign eventually approves and publishes to contain the corrected endpoint. Her manager suggests waiting until approval and fixing it afterwards to avoid delays, and the team has already prepared App Center screenshots. Which two steps should Amara take? (Select two)

options.text: Create a new draft version that contains the fix alongside the In Review version, and ask Docusign to review the newer draft instead
Cancel the publishing request so the version reverts to Draft status, and then correct the params.uri value in the registration
Edit the params.uri value directly on the In Review version, because the reviewers always evaluate the most recently saved registration details
Resubmit the corrected version for review, because after cancelling, the version is a Draft that cannot be published unreviewed
Delete the In Review version and register a separate app with the corrected endpoint under the same app name before resubmitting

answerText: Cancel the publishing request so the version reverts to Draft status, and then correct the params.uri value in the registration; Resubmit the corrected version for review, because after cancelling, the version is a Draft that cannot be published unreviewed
explanation: A version that is In Review cannot be updated or deleted until the publishing process is cancelled, which reverts it to Draft; after updating it, it must be resubmitted for review before it can be published.
whyNotOthers: B and D are right because cancelling returns the version to Draft so it can be edited, and the edited Draft must be resubmitted for review. The trap is A: you cannot create a new draft version while another version is in Draft, In Review, Approved or Rejected status. C fails because updating is prohibited in In Review, and E fails because deleting is also prohibited in In Review and app names must be unique.

optionExplanations.A: Only one version can be in Draft, In Review, Approved or Rejected at a time, so a new draft cannot be created alongside the In Review version.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Cancelling the publishing process reverts the version to Draft, which is the only way to update it.
optionExplanations.C: Updating a version is prohibited while it is In Review; the version must first revert to Draft.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. After updating the reverted Draft, it must be resubmitted for review before it can be published.
optionExplanations.E: Deleting is prohibited in In Review, and a second registration with the same unique app name is not allowed.

decode.needs: Cancel publishing to return to Draft, edit, then resubmit
clues: shows In Review and needs a fix -> cancel the publishing process first
the approved version must contain the fix -> resubmit for review
manager's wait-and-fix idea, screenshots ready -> red herrings

concept.title: Cancel review to edit a version
concept.line: An In Review, Approved or Rejected version must be cancelled back to Draft to edit, then resubmitted for review.

stem: Which extension points support the phone verification extension?

options.text: eSignature Add Fields view and Signing only
eSignature Add Fields view and Signing, and Maestro workflows
Web Forms only
eSignature Add Fields view and Signing, and Web Forms

answerText: eSignature Add Fields view and Signing, and Web Forms
explanation: Phone verification, like email address verification, is supported at the eSignature Add Fields view and Signing and also in Web Forms.
whyNotOthers: D is right because phone and email verification are the two data verification extensions that also work in Web Forms. The trap is A: that is the extension point for the other verification types such as bank account, SSN, FEIN and postal address. B swaps Web Forms for Maestro workflows, which are the extension point for Data IO and file output, and C drops eSignature.

optionExplanations.A: This is true for bank account, SSN, FEIN and postal address verification, but phone verification is also available in Web Forms.
optionExplanations.B: Maestro workflows are the extension point for Data IO and file output cloud storage; phone verification's second extension point is Web Forms.
optionExplanations.C: Phone verification also works in eSignature Add Fields view and Signing.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. Phone and email verification support eSignature Add Fields view and Signing plus Web Forms.

concept.title: Email and phone verification reach Web Forms
concept.line: Email and phone verification work in eSignature and Web Forms; other data verification types are eSignature only.

stem: Tessera Analytics, a small software vendor that has never joined the Docusign partner program, has built an address-cleansing extension app with a team of three developers. Its business goal is for any Docusign customer in the United States to discover the app while browsing the App Center and install it without contacting Tessera first. The app passes its connection, extension and functional tests in Tessera's developer account. The product owner wants the route that reaches that goal without having to re-register the app later. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Register the app with PUBLIC distribution and submit it for review; Docusign onboards Tessera into the partner program as part of that submission
Register the app with PRIVATE distribution now, then switch the distribution to PUBLIC after the first live release, once partner onboarding has been completed
Register the app with PRIVATE distribution and share the live app with each customer's production account as that customer asks to use it
Give each customer the app manifest so their administrator can register a copy in the Developer Console and install it in their own account

answerText: Register the app with PUBLIC distribution and submit it for review; Docusign onboards Tessera into the partner program as part of that submission
explanation: Publishing a public app requires being a Docusign partner, and if you are not yet a partner Docusign works with you on partner program onboarding when you submit the app for review. 'Any customer can discover it in the App Center' means PUBLIC distribution.
whyNotOthers: A is right because public distribution is what makes the app discoverable by every customer, and partner onboarding happens with the review submission. The trap is B: the distribution type cannot be changed once the app is Live, so this would force a new registration. C requires manual sharing (up to 20 production accounts, each admin approving) and gives no browsing discovery, and D is not how customers obtain apps; they install them from the App Center.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Public distribution gives App Center discovery to all customers, and Docusign handles partner onboarding when a non-partner submits for review.
optionExplanations.B: Distribution cannot be modified once the app is Live, so switching later would mean registering a new app.
optionExplanations.C: Private apps are shared with a limited list of production accounts whose admins must approve them; customers cannot discover them by browsing.
optionExplanations.D: Customers install apps from the App Center; handing out a manifest to re-register is not the distribution model.

decode.needs: PUBLIC distribution, with partner onboarding at review submission
clues: any customer can discover and install it -> PUBLIC distribution
never joined the partner program -> onboarding happens at review submission
without re-registering later -> distribution cannot change once Live
three developers -> red herring

concept.title: Public apps need the partner program
concept.line: Public App Center listing requires Docusign partnership; non-partners are onboarded when they submit for review, and distribution is fixed once Live.

stem: When a private extension app becomes Live, with up to how many production accounts can the developer share it?
explanation: For a private extension app, the developer provides a list of up to 20 production accounts to share the live app with.
whyNotOthers: C is right: private sharing is capped at 20 production accounts. The trap is B, a common guess for a small allow-list; A and D are not documented limits either.

optionExplanations.A: Not the documented limit; private apps can be shared with more accounts than this.
optionExplanations.B: Plausible but wrong; the documented limit is higher.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A private app can be shared with up to 20 production accounts.
optionExplanations.D: Exceeds the documented limit for private sharing.

concept.title: Private apps: up to 20 accounts
concept.line: A Live private extension app is shared with a list of up to 20 production accounts, each approved by its admin.

topic: Testing an app served from a laptop
stem: Kenji is prototyping a postal address verification app on his laptop before the hosting team provisions a server. The external provider's OAuth service is cloud hosted, so the connection test in the Developer Console succeeds, but every extension test fails because the endpoint cannot be reached. Each action's params.uri currently points at http://localhost:3000. His laptop runs Chrome with the corporate VPN switched off, and the provider's responses already match the Docusign action contract. What should Kenji do to keep testing locally?

options.text: Keep localhost in params.uri and run the extension tests from a browser on the same laptop, because the Developer Console sends the test requests from the browser
Expose the local service through a tunnel such as ngrok and put the public HTTPS tunnel URL in each action's params.uri, because Docusign's servers make the calls
Reinstall the app in his developer account after each change so that the updated params.uri values are picked up before he reruns the extension tests
Build an API proxy on the laptop that maps requests to the Docusign action contract, and point each action's params.uri at the proxy's localhost port

answerText: Expose the local service through a tunnel such as ngrok and put the public HTTPS tunnel URL in each action's params.uri, because Docusign's servers make the calls
explanation: Extension tests are executed from the Docusign platform directly to the external endpoints, so Docusign servers need a public URL. Docusign recommends a tunnel such as ngrok to expose a locally running app while developing.
whyNotOthers: B is right because a tunnel gives Docusign a public URL that reaches the laptop. The trap is A: extension tests are not sent from the browser but from the Docusign platform, so localhost is unreachable. C fails because registration updates are applied automatically to the installed app, and D is unnecessary because the responses already match the contract and a localhost proxy is still unreachable.

optionExplanations.A: Extension tests run from the Docusign platform to the endpoint, so localhost on Kenji's laptop is never reachable.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. A tunnel such as ngrok exposes the local app at a public URL that Docusign's servers can call.
optionExplanations.C: Updates to the registration are applied automatically to the installed version; reinstalling does not fix reachability.
optionExplanations.D: A proxy is needed only when the API does not match the action contract, and a localhost proxy is just as unreachable.

decode.needs: A public URL (tunnel) for the locally running endpoints
clues: connection test passes but extension tests cannot reach the endpoint -> endpoint not publicly reachable
before the hosting team provisions a server -> keep running locally, so tunnel
responses already match the contract -> no API proxy needed
Chrome, VPN off -> red herrings

concept.title: Docusign must reach a public endpoint
concept.line: Docusign servers call extension endpoints directly, so local development needs a public tunnel URL such as ngrok.

stem: Northgate Archives sells a cloud vault and is building an extension app so customers can save completed agreements into it as a step in their Maestro workflows. Customer feedback is clear: when configuring the step, workflow designers want to pick the target drive and then browse to a folder, instead of typing a storage path by hand. Many of these customers also sync deal data with Salesforce. Northgate is a new app, not an update of an existing one. How should Northgate design the extension?

options.text: Use the file output cloud storage extension with only its required write-file action, because Maestro discovers the provider's drives and folders on its own
Use the file archive extension, because it is the file extension type that lets the workflow designer browse destinations in the storage provider
Use a Data IO extension whose Search Records action returns folders as records, so the designer can search for the destination while configuring the step
Use the file output cloud storage extension with its required write-file action plus the optional ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities

answerText: Use the file output cloud storage extension with its required write-file action plus the optional ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities
explanation: File output cloud storage is the extension for new apps that write documents to cloud storage from Maestro workflows. Capabilities are optional extras; the List Drives capability returns the storage drives so the workflow preparer can select one, and List Directory Contents supports browsing folders.
whyNotOthers: D is right because the required write action stores the file, and the optional capabilities give designers the drive and folder pickers they asked for. The trap is A: capabilities are optional, so without them nothing provides the drive list. B fails because file archive is the legacy extension that new apps should not use, and C misuses Data IO, which reads and writes system-of-record data rather than storing files.

optionExplanations.A: Capabilities are optional and must be implemented; without List Drives there is nothing for the designer to pick from.
optionExplanations.B: File archive is legacy; new extension apps should use file output cloud storage.
optionExplanations.C: Data IO moves structured data to and from a system of record; it is not the file storage extension.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The write-file action is required, and the ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities let the preparer pick a drive and folder.

decode.needs: File output cloud storage with ListDrives and ListDirectoryContents capabilities
clues: save completed agreements as a workflow step -> file output cloud storage in Maestro
pick the drive and browse to a folder -> optional capabilities
new app -> not the legacy file archive extension
Salesforce sync -> red herring

concept.title: Capabilities add optional extension features
concept.line: Extensions require their contract actions; optional capabilities, like List Drives for file output, add features such as destination pickers.

topic: Default regions for a public app
stem: A public extension app is published without any additional regions being specified. Which accounts can install it from the production App Center?

options.text: Only accounts based in the US
Accounts in every Docusign region
Only accounts the developer lists at publication
Only accounts in the developer's own region

answerText: Only accounts based in the US
explanation: By default, published extension apps are available only to US customers on the production App Center; other regions must be added explicitly.
whyNotOthers: A is right because availability defaults to the US. The trap is B: global availability is not the default, so regions beyond the US must be specified. C describes private distribution, and D is not how the default is defined.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Published extension apps default to US customers only; other regions must be added.
optionExplanations.B: Additional regions must be specified explicitly; they are not included by default.
optionExplanations.C: Listing specific accounts is how private apps are shared, not public ones.
optionExplanations.D: The default is the US, not the developer's own region.

concept.title: Public apps default to US only
concept.line: A published public extension app is installable only by US accounts unless additional publication regions are specified.

topic: Functional test for a Data IO app
stem: Pinewood Insurance's QA lead must reproduce what a real end user will experience with the company's new Data IO extension app before it is submitted for review. The app reads policyholder details from the policy administration system to prefill a form and writes any changes back. Connection and extension tests have already passed in the developer account. The policy team keeps its standard forms as eSignature templates, and the QA lead has a budget of two days. Which approach should the QA lead take?

options.text: Add the app's fields to an eSignature template, send an envelope to herself, and fill in the fields as a signer would to trigger the read and write actions
Build a Maestro workflow with a web form derived from the policy eSignature template between a data read step and a data write step, then run an instance
Create and publish a Maestro workflow with a data read step, a standalone web form step and a data write step, then execute an instance of the workflow
Rerun the extension tests for Search Records, Create Record and Patch Record from App Testing, since they replay the end-user flow for each action

answerText: Create and publish a Maestro workflow with a data read step, a standalone web form step and a data write step, then execute an instance of the workflow
explanation: Functional tests simulate the end-user experience, and for Data IO the supported functional test is a Maestro workflow test. The web form used in that workflow must be standalone; web forms derived from eSignature templates cannot be used in workflows.
whyNotOthers: C is right because Data IO is tested functionally through a workflow instance with read, standalone web form and write steps. The trap is B: it uses the right test type, but a web form derived from an eSignature template cannot be used in a workflow. A fails because the envelope test is not supported for Data IO, and D fails because extension tests are integration tests that call endpoints directly rather than simulating the end user.

optionExplanations.A: The envelope functional test is not supported for Data IO; Data IO runs in Maestro workflows.
optionExplanations.B: Right test type, but web forms derived from eSignature templates cannot be used in workflows; the form must be standalone.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. A workflow instance with read, standalone web form and write steps is the Data IO functional test.
optionExplanations.D: Extension tests call endpoints from the Docusign platform directly; they do not simulate the end-user experience.

decode.needs: A Maestro workflow functional test with a standalone web form
clues: reproduce what a real end user will experience -> functional test, not integration test
reads to prefill a form and writes back -> Data IO read and write steps in Maestro
standard forms kept as eSignature templates -> template-derived web forms cannot be used in workflows
two-day budget -> red herring

concept.title: Data IO functional tests use workflows
concept.line: Data IO and file output are functionally tested in Maestro workflows; connected fields and data verification in envelopes.

stem: Halcyon runs an append-only compliance ledger: entries are never edited once written. Its Maestro onboarding workflow must add one new ledger entry each time an onboarding finishes, and nothing is ever read back into the workflow. To cut development time, the developer proposes declaring as few Data IO actions as possible. The ledger exposes a JSON API that already matches the Docusign contracts, and the app will be private. The workflow already includes an identity verification step before signing. What should the developer implement?

options.text: Only Create Record, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions, because a create-only extension never searches for or patches an existing record
All five Data IO actions, with full logic in Create Record, while Patch Record must still be defined but does not need to contain any code
Search Records, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions with the Data Read option, and send each new entry in the body of the search request
Create Record, Patch Record, Get Type Names and Get Type Definitions, omitting Search Records because no existing entry is ever looked up

answerText: All five Data IO actions, with full logic in Create Record, while Patch Record must still be defined but does not need to contain any code
explanation: Data output cannot be standalone because it uses the data input actions to find records, so writing requires all five Data IO actions. If the app only creates records, only Create Record needs a full implementation; Patch Record must still be defined but needs no code.
whyNotOthers: B is right because a writing Data IO app must declare all five actions, with Patch Record allowed to be an empty definition for a create-only system. The trap is D: Search Records cannot be omitted because data output relies on the input actions. A omits both Search and Patch, and C is a read-only registration that cannot write at all.

optionExplanations.A: Writing requires all five actions; Search Records and Patch Record cannot be dropped.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. All five actions are declared; for create-only, Create Record is fully implemented and Patch Record can be an empty definition.
optionExplanations.C: Data Read registers a read-only app; Search Records does not create entries.
optionExplanations.D: Data output uses the data input actions to find records, so Search Records must be implemented.

decode.needs: All five Data IO actions, with Patch Record as an empty definition
clues: append-only ledger, entries never edited -> create-only, Patch Record needs no code
add one new entry per onboarding -> data output (write) requires all five actions
JSON API matches contracts, private app -> red herrings

concept.title: Data IO writes need all five actions
concept.line: Data output cannot be standalone; a create-only app implements all five actions, with Patch Record defined but code-free.

stem: In which status can an extension app version be deleted directly in the Developer Console?

options.text: Draft
Rejected
Approved
Live

explanation: An extension app version can only be deleted when it is in Draft status.
whyNotOthers: A is right: only Draft versions can be deleted. The trap is B: a Rejected version must first have its publishing request cancelled so it reverts to Draft. C has the same restriction, and a Live version cannot be deleted at all.

optionExplanations.A: Correct. Deletion is allowed only in Draft status.
optionExplanations.B: Rejected is still part of the review process; cancel publishing to revert to Draft before deleting.
optionExplanations.C: Approved versions must be cancelled back to Draft before they can be deleted.
optionExplanations.D: Live versions cannot be deleted; removing a live app requires help through the Developer Community.

concept.title: Only Draft versions can be deleted
concept.line: Delete only Draft versions; cancel publishing to revert In Review, Approved or Rejected versions; Live versions cannot be deleted.

stem: Ridgeview Health has contracted Coastal Integrators, a Docusign partner, to build an extension app that checks patient record numbers against the hospital's proprietary clinical system while forms are signed. Only Ridgeview's US production accounts will ever use it, so it will be a private app. Coastal's project manager writes down the assumptions for the rollout plan, noting that the hospital's own IT team also wants to try the app in its developer account. Which two assumptions are correct? (Select two)

options.text: Because the app is private, it can be published without any Docusign review, since that review applies only to apps listed for all customers
Docusign must still approve the private app before publication, although the approval guidelines are less stringent than for public apps
After publication, Coastal can also share the private app with the hospital's developer accounts so the IT team can try it there
If other hospitals ask for the app later, Coastal can switch the Live app's distribution to public without registering it again
An administrator of each shared production account must approve the private app before any user there can install and use it

answerText: Docusign must still approve the private app before publication, although the approval guidelines are less stringent than for public apps; An administrator of each shared production account must approve the private app before any user there can install and use it
explanation: Private extension apps still need Docusign approval before publication (with less stringent guidelines), and each production account's administrator must approve the shared app before its users can install it.
whyNotOthers: B and E are right: review still applies to private apps, and account admins approve shared private apps. The trap is C: private apps can be shared with additional production accounts but not with additional developer accounts. A is wrong because publishing still requires approval, and D is wrong because distribution cannot be changed once the app is Live.

optionExplanations.A: Private apps are not visible to all customers, but Docusign still must approve them before publication.
optionExplanations.B: Correct. Private apps go through Docusign approval, with guidelines less stringent than for public apps.
optionExplanations.C: Private apps can be shared with additional production accounts, not with additional developer accounts.
optionExplanations.D: Distribution type cannot be modified once the app is Live.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. An administrator of each production account must approve the private app before anyone in the account can use it.

decode.needs: Private distribution rules: review, admin approval, production accounts only
clues: only the hospital's own production accounts -> private distribution
built by a contracted partner -> partners can build private apps for customers
IT team wants it in its developer account -> private apps cannot be shared with other developer accounts

concept.title: Private apps: review plus admin approval
concept.line: Private apps still pass Docusign review, are shared only with production accounts, and each account admin must approve them.

stem: Lucia is preparing the Developer Console integration testing plan for her team's connected fields app, which verifies customer IDs against their CRM. The CRM's OAuth server and API are both reachable on public HTTPS endpoints, and the app has been installed to her developer account. The plan will be reviewed by an architect who often asks why the order matters. She will change the registration several times while testing, and the CRM team wants the results by Friday. Which two statements belong in her plan? (Select two)

options.text: After every change to the registration, uninstall and reinstall the app in the developer account so the tests use the updated values
Run the extension tests before configuring the connection, because they only check that each action endpoint answers on its configured URL
Run the connection test first, signing in with the authorization provider's credentials, because extension tests reuse that authorization
Treat passing extension tests as proof of the signer's experience, because they call the endpoints from inside a test envelope
Expect extension tests to call each action's params.uri from the Docusign platform and confirm the response format

answerText: Run the connection test first, signing in with the authorization provider's credentials, because extension tests reuse that authorization; Expect extension tests to call each action's params.uri from the Docusign platform and confirm the response format
explanation: A connection test obtains authorization using the provider credentials you supply, and extension tests use that authorization, so the connection test must pass first. Extension tests call each action's endpoint from the Docusign platform and confirm the response format.
whyNotOthers: C and E are right because they describe the required order and what extension tests actually check. The trap is A: updates to the registration are applied automatically to the installed version, so no reinstall is needed. B reverses the required order, and D confuses integration tests with functional tests, which are the ones that exercise envelopes or workflows.

optionExplanations.A: Registration updates are applied automatically to the installed app; reinstalling is unnecessary.
optionExplanations.B: A successful connection test is required before extension tests can run.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. The connection test obtains authorization with the provider credentials, and extension tests reuse it.
optionExplanations.D: Extension tests call endpoints directly; the signer experience is checked by functional tests.
optionExplanations.E: Correct. Extension tests send requests to each params.uri from the Docusign platform and check the response format.

decode.needs: The integration test order and what each test checks
clues: why the order matters -> extension tests reuse the connection test's authorization
will change the registration several times -> updates apply automatically, no reinstall
public HTTPS endpoints -> red herring here, endpoints are reachable

concept.title: Connection test before extension tests
concept.line: Connection tests obtain authorization that extension tests reuse; registration updates apply automatically to the installed app.

topic: Extension template value for Data IO
stem: In an app manifest for a Data IO app, which value belongs in extensions.template?

options.text: DataIO.Version6.SearchRecords
DataIO.Version6.GetTypeDefinitions
DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput
FileIO.Version1.FileOutputCloudStorage

explanation: For a Data IO app registered by manifest, extensions.template is DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput; values such as DataIO.Version6.SearchRecords go in actions.template.
whyNotOthers: C is right because the extension contract for Data IO is DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput. The trap is A: SearchRecords is an action contract value used in actions.template, not the extension template. B is also an action value, and D is the extension template for file output cloud storage.

optionExplanations.A: This is an action contract value used in actions.template.
optionExplanations.B: This is an action contract value used in actions.template.
optionExplanations.C: Correct. DataIO.Version6.DataInputOutput is the Data IO extension contract set in extensions.template.
optionExplanations.D: This is the extension template for file output cloud storage, not Data IO.

concept.title: Extension template versus action template
concept.line: extensions.template names the extension contract; actions.template names an action contract, such as DataIO.Version6.SearchRecords.

stem: Brightline, a Docusign partner, has a Live public extension app installed by about 300 customer accounts. Product management wants to add a phone verification extension to the same app. Customers must keep using the current app without interruption while the change goes through, and should not have to do anything to receive the new version. Brightline's sales team also wants to announce the feature at a conference next month, and the support desk is preparing a short help article. Which approach should Brightline follow?

options.text: Edit the Live version in place; registration changes to a Live app apply immediately to installed accounts, so customers get the new extension with no further review
Delete the Live version and register a new app that contains both extensions, then ask the 300 customers to install the new listing from the App Center
Update the registration, which creates a new Draft version; after review and publishing, the old version is Discontinued and each customer admin reinstalls the new one
Update the registration to create a new Draft version; once reviewed and published, the old version is Discontinued and installs upgrade automatically

answerText: Update the registration to create a new Draft version; once reviewed and published, the old version is Discontinued and installs upgrade automatically
explanation: Updating a Live app's registration creates a new Draft version that must be reviewed and published. On publication the new version becomes Live, the previous one becomes Discontinued, and accounts that had it installed are automatically upgraded.
whyNotOthers: D is right because versioning keeps the current Live version running during review and upgrades installed accounts automatically. The trap is C: it describes the same flow but wrongly requires admins to reinstall, which contradicts 'should not have to do anything'. A skips the new version and review, and B is impossible because a Live version cannot be deleted and would force customers to reinstall.

optionExplanations.A: Updating a Live app creates a new Draft version that must pass review; nothing changes in place.
optionExplanations.B: Live versions cannot be deleted, and customers would have to reinstall a new listing.
optionExplanations.C: Same versioning flow, but installed accounts are upgraded automatically; admins do not need to reinstall.
optionExplanations.D: Correct. The new version goes through review and publishing, the old one becomes Discontinued, and installed accounts are upgraded automatically.

decode.needs: Extension app versioning: new Draft, review, publish, automatic upgrade
clues: add an extension to a Live app -> update registration, new Draft version
keep using it without interruption -> Live version stays until the new one is published
should not have to do anything -> installed accounts are upgraded automatically
conference next month -> red herring

concept.title: Live app updates create new versions
concept.line: Updating a Live app creates a Draft version; once published, the old version is Discontinued and installs upgrade automatically.
